newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Volvo trucks drive home weak result.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Volvo trucks drive home weak result.

text.p: Swedish vehicle maker AB Volvo on Wednesday reported weaker-than-expected earnings for the first nine months of 1996 despite significant capital gains.
Industry analysts said they were disappointed by a below par performance by its its American truck operation and the group's shares slipped lower.
A 12 percent rise in pre-tax profit to 12.03 billion crowns ($1.83 billion) was entirely due to capital gains on share sales, while sales fell 12 percent to 113.6 billion crowns.
Operating profit plunged to 2.32 billion crowns from 8.84 billion. There was a 600 million crown boost from positive currency effects in the nine months.
"Lower sales, depressed prices and higher production and product development costs were the main reasons for the decline," chief executive Soren Gyll said in the nine-month results statement.

But he said results were not as bad as they seemed at first sight, commenting: "The weak operating profit during the period does not reflect the group's strategic position. Volvo Cars and Volvo Trucks have very competitive product programmes today."
Results were buoyed by the sale of a stake in U.S./Swedish drugs group Pharmacia & Upjohn, which gave a capital gain of 7.8 billion crowns.
Analysts said the result was a disappointment. The stock market had anticipated pre-tax profits of 12.79 billion crowns.
"Profits in the car sector were slightly better than expected but the truck sector was worse and that is worrying," analyst Philip Ayton from BZW told Reuters.
"However, this does seem to be a trend in the whole industry. I think the third quarter was the low point so we should start to see some improvement from now on."
As foreshadowed by the group, Volvo Truck's performance was a major handicap, suffering from weak demand in North and South America, although European deliveries rose by six percent.
Truck sales fell 14 percent to 32.71 billion crowns, while operating income dived to 413 million crowns from 4.03 billion.
"The order backlog at September 30, 1996 was 40 percent lower than on the same date a year earlier, primarily due to lower demand in North and South America," Gyll said.
But Gyll said half of a 1.4 billion crown loss in North America was due to costs for phasing out a plant in Ohio and realigning costs for phasing out existing products.
Analyst Keith Hayes from Goldman Sachs said the market had not known exactly how hard the truck operation had been hit.

"It is not an easy operating environment and I don't see it getting any easier for them," Hayes said. "But I think the really worrying thing is if you look at cash flow. It is negative excluding capital gains."
Volvo's Car division showed a drop in operating income to 573 million crowns from 1.93 billion with sales income falling to 59.83 billion from 63.15 billion a year earlier.

"Volvo Cars' income level is unsatisfactory but is developing positively," Gyll said. "This is an effect of the cost rationalisation measures implemented and increased revenues from the Volvo S40 and V40."

Analysts were cautiously forecasting that Volvo had now hit bottom. "I would expect some improvement over the coming year, unless there is a recession somewhere in the world. So this is bottom," said Hayes.
Volvo's share price fell four crowns when the Stockholm bourse opened but at 1000 GMT was three crowns lower at 138.
($1=6.58 crowns)
